title: Sixpence a Night
passage:
Owlerby's pound was a roofless square of wall behind the church, and any beast found straying on the common was shut in it, at its owner's charge, until he came. The pinder's office carried no wage: Jabez Skellorne had the fees instead, and worked at the smithy between times. The vestry's table of 1846 charged a shilling for taking up a beast and sixpence a night for its keep. Notice was another matter. Skellorne was to cry what he held at the church door each Sunday after service, and nowhere else. Farmers on the far side of the common heard of a beast no other way. In 1851 a heifer taken up on a Monday cost its owner four shillings; another, taken up on the Saturday of that same week, cost one and sixpence. Both were fetched on the Sunday they were cried, and neither owner disputed the reckoning. The table hung on the pound door until the wall came down in 1903.
– Aveline Hemblow

questions.prompt: What is implied here about the pound at Owlerby?

options.text: The pound was probably a useful source of income for the parish in these years.
An owner's bill turned on which day of the week his beast was taken up.
Because the table charged by the night, a heavy bill marked an owner slow to miss his beast.
Skellorne decided how long a beast stayed in the pound, and a longer stay paid him better.

questions.rationale: TYPE-002, one_inch_inference. Three facts are stated separately and never joined. (i) The charge is partly a standing fee and partly a running one: 'a shilling for taking up a beast and sixpence a night for its keep'. (ii) The only notice was weekly and fixed: Skellorne 'was to cry what he held at the church door each Sunday after service, and nowhere else', and 'Farmers on the far side of the common heard of a beast no other way'. (iii) Two bills are given for the same week - a heifer taken up on the Monday cost four shillings, another taken up on the Saturday cost one and sixpence - and 'Both were fetched on the Sunday they were cried', so the owners behaved identically. Joining these gives B: since the running part of the charge accrued until the next crying, and the crying came once a week, what an owner paid was fixed by how far his beast's capture fell from Sunday. The numbers reconcile exactly at the table's rates (Monday capture: six nights, 12d + 36d = 48d = four shillings; Saturday capture: one night, 12d + 6d = 18d = one and sixpence), but the reader does not need the arithmetic - only the direction. The passage never draws the conclusion and nobody in it comments, which is what makes the item an inference rather than retrieval. A = scope-shift onto the wrong beneficiary, and the only hedged option in the set. Fees look like revenue, and 'probably' makes the claim modest enough to feel safe; but the passage removes the parish from the money in one clause - 'The pinder's office carried no wage: Jabez Skellorne had the fees instead' - so the fees were the pinder's pay, not parish income, and the text gives no parish receipts at all. C = half-right conjunction, the strongest rival. Its premise is straight from the table (the charge did run by the night), which lends borrowed credibility to the verdict glued onto it; but the passage says nothing about when either owner missed his beast, and it forecloses the reading twice - notice ran through the Sunday crying and no other channel, and both beasts were in fact fetched on the same Sunday. A reader who stops at the comma takes it. D = agency swap: the fees were the pinder's, so a long stay did pay him better, and it is tempting to hand him the decision that produced it. The text withholds exactly that: he 'was to cry what he held ... each Sunday after service, and nowhere else', an obligation on a fixed day, so the length of a stay followed from the calendar rather than from his choice. Hedge balance: the key is a flat, unhedged assertion and the one cautious-sounding option (A) is wrong, so 'pick the qualified answer' scores nothing here. No option carries an absolutizer. Measured with mech.py tokenize the key runs 16 tokens against A 15, C 18 and D 17 - second shortest, never the longest.
